intro:
By the end of this track you can say why a payments system keeps some of its data outside tables, and pick a model for each access pattern: key-value with a sort key, wide-column, document, property graph, or triples and rules. You can turn a list of access patterns into DynamoDB and Cassandra keys, size a Cassandra partition, shape a MongoDB document and say when a PostgreSQL `jsonb` column would do instead, walk a graph with a recursive CTE, SQL/PGQ or Cypher, evaluate recursive Datalog rules, and count the calls a GraphQL server makes.

Take the SQL track first. Lesson 1 starts from what the relational model makes hard, and later lessons compare against `jsonb` and recursive CTEs. How these stores spread data over machines, keep copies and run transactions comes later, in the Partitioning, Replication and Transactions tracks; when a lesson needs one of those ideas, it gives it in a sentence and points ahead.

The labs are Kotlin, in `labs/nosql` (lesson 7's are SQL files in `labs/sql`). Lessons 1, 2, 5 and 9 are plain-Kotlin models that test in a second. Lessons 3, 4, 6, 7 and 8 run against real stores that Testcontainers starts (DynamoDB Local, MongoDB 9.0, PostgreSQL 18, Neo4j 2026.10) and need Docker. The Try-its use Compose files in `labs/env` (`dynamodb.yml`, `cassandra.yml`, `mongo.yml`, `mongo-rs.yml`, `postgres.yml`, `neo4j.yml`): run one at a time from the `labs` folder and stop it with `down -v`. `./gradlew :nosql:test --tests 'sfz.model.lNN.*'` runs one lesson's lab, and `:sql:` instead of `:nosql:` for lesson 7.
cheatsheet:
## Why other models exist (lesson 1)

Tables make three things hard: changing the shape of records (every row has the same columns), keeping related data together (locality), and growing past one machine. Each family gives up joins, multi-row transactions or a declared schema to make one of them cheap.

| | Schema-on-write | Schema-on-read |
|---|---|---|
| Who checks the shape | the database, on every write | every reader, in code |
| Example | a table; a `CHECK` on `jsonb`; MongoDB 9.0 `constraint` | a document store with no validator |
| Wins when | every record has the same structure | records really differ (forms per country, partner payloads) |

## The families

| Family | You store | You find it by | Example in the track |
|---|---|---|---|
| Key-value | a value, or an item of named attributes | its key, or a sorted run in one partition | DynamoDB (lessons 3, 4) |
| Wide-column (not columnar) | partitions of sorted rows, columns per row | partition key, then a slice of clustering columns | Cassandra 5.0 (lesson 5) |
| Document | JSON-like trees | any indexed field | MongoDB 9.0, PostgreSQL `jsonb` (lesson 6) |
| Property graph | nodes and relationships, both with properties | a start node, then a walk | SQL/PGQ (lesson 7), Neo4j 2026.10 (lesson 8) |
| Triples and rules | subject, predicate, object; recursive rules | triple patterns, rules run to a fixpoint | RDF, SPARQL, Datalog (lesson 9) |

Search, time-series and vector stores are mostly one special index over these models (Stonebraker and Pavlo: a vector store is a document store plus a nearest-neighbour index). Bigtable sorts keys and cuts them into ranges; Dynamo hashes keys onto a ring and copies each to N nodes. DynamoDB is not Dynamo: each partition has a Multi-Paxos leader.

## Keys come from the questions (lessons 2 to 5)

- Write every access pattern down with its rate before choosing a key.
- Partition key: `=` on all its parts; it picks the partition. Sort key or clustering columns: sorted inside the partition; `=` on leading parts, then one range, no gaps.
- Every query is a key lookup, a range read or a scan. A filter runs after the read and pays for everything read.
- A pattern the key can't answer gets another copy: a DynamoDB GSI (eventually consistent), another Cassandra table, another MongoDB index. Each copy costs a write.
- DynamoDB: a read unit is 4 KB strongly consistent, a write unit 1 KB; each partition tops out at 3,000 reads and 1,000 writes a second; items are at most 400 KB. Single-table design stores a screen's join under one partition key.
- Cassandra partition: under 100,000 rows and 100 MB. Rows = write rate × bucket length, so add a time bucket sized for the busiest key.

## Writes that can't race

| Need | DynamoDB | Cassandra | MongoDB | PostgreSQL `jsonb` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Insert once | `attribute_not_exists(pk)` | `INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS` (Paxos) | unique (partial) index | primary key, `ON CONFLICT` |
| Check and change one record | condition expression | `UPDATE ... IF` | guarded `updateOne` filter | guarded `UPDATE ... WHERE` |
| Several records | `TransactWriteItems`, 100 items, 4 MB, 2 writes per item | logged batch (atomic, not isolated) | multi-document transaction | any transaction |

Cassandra deletes are tombstones kept for `gc_grace_seconds` (10 days); a read warns past 1,000 and fails past 100,000. Don't use a partition as a queue.

## Graphs (lessons 7 to 9)

- `WITH RECURSIVE`: the anchor runs once, the recursive term reads only the previous round (the working table) until a round is empty. PostgreSQL has no depth limit and no cycle detection: use `CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path`.
- SQL/PGQ (SQL:2023): `CREATE PROPERTY GRAPH` over tables, `GRAPH_TABLE (g MATCH ... COLUMNS ...)`. Ships in Oracle 23ai and 26ai, Spanner Graph, DuckDB via `duckpgq`. Not in PostgreSQL 18 or 19.
- Cypher 25: `(a:Account)-[:USES]->(x)`, quantified paths `((...)-[...]->(...)){1,3}`, `-[:TRANSFERRED_TO]->{3,6}`. Start from a uniqueness constraint (`NodeUniqueIndexSeek`); bound every walk; keep supernodes out.
- GQL (ISO/IEC 39075:2024) standardized the Cypher pattern style; Cypher 25 covers most mandatory features.
- RDF triples with IRIs; a SPARQL query is a join of triple patterns; `ex:owns+` walks any depth. RDF 1.2 is a W3C Candidate Recommendation (April 2026).
- Datalog: `controls(X, Z) :- controls(X, Y), owns(Y, Z).` Semi-naive evaluation joins only the last round's new facts, which is PostgreSQL's working table.
- GraphQL is an API query language over any backend: one resolver per field makes 1 + N + N calls; a loader per level makes one call per level.
recap: The relational model makes changing shape, locality and scale-out hard. Every other model trades away joins, multi-row transactions or a declared schema to make one of them cheap.
Schemaless means schema-on-read: the reader carries the schema. MongoDB 9.0's `constraint` level and PostgreSQL `jsonb` with CHECK constraints show the two worlds converging.
Design keys from the access patterns: each one should be a key lookup or a range read, and every extra copy (GSI, query table, index) costs a write.

DynamoDB is a hash map of sorted item collections with per-partition limits (3,000 RCU, 1,000 WCU, 400 KB items); single-table design stores a screen's join under one key, and TransactWriteItems makes up to 100 writes one unit.
Cassandra's wide-column model is partitions of sorted rows, not columnar storage. Size partitions with time buckets, and remember that deletes are tombstones.

A document puts what's read and changed together into one atomically updated record. A PostgreSQL `jsonb` column gives the same model next to joins and transactions; MongoDB adds path indexes and sharding.
Graph questions of unknown depth need recursion: WITH RECURSIVE (with CYCLE), SQL/PGQ in Oracle, Spanner and DuckDB, or Cypher 25 in Neo4j, whose pattern style GQL standardized.
RDF triples and SPARQL treat a query as a join of patterns; Datalog's recursive rules evaluate semi-naively to a fixpoint; GraphQL is an API language whose N+1 resolver calls need batching.

quiz.q: A team wants to move merchant onboarding forms, which differ by country and change every quarter, off a table with 140 mostly-NULL columns. Which statement about a document store is accurate?
options: It removes the need for a schema
It moves the schema into the code that reads the documents, unless a validator holds the shared fields to rules
It rewrites old documents automatically when the shape changes
It can't store documents with different fields in one collection
quiz.why: A document store is schema-on-read by default: each reader must handle every shape ever written. A validator (in MongoDB 9.0, even at the `constraint` level) puts schema-on-write back for the fields you name. Nothing rewrites old documents for you (lesson 1).

quiz.q: A DynamoDB table has partition key `accountId` and sort key `createdAt`. Which request is one Query that reads only what it returns?
options: `merchantId = M-0042`, newest first
`accountId = A-1001 AND amountMinor > 5000`
`accountId = A-1001 AND createdAt BETWEEN 08:00 AND 12:00`
`createdAt > 09:00` for every account
quiz.why: It gives the partition key with `=` and one range on the sort key: one contiguous slice. A filter on `amountMinor` still reads the whole partition, and the other two don't name a partition at all (lessons 2 and 3).

quiz.q: A running-total item for one merchant (one partition key, one sort key, under 1 KB) is updated 1,200 times a second. What happens in DynamoDB?
options: Writes beyond about 1,000 a second are throttled, whatever the table's capacity
Nothing, as long as the table's provisioned capacity is above 1,200 write units
DynamoDB splits the item over two partitions to absorb the load
The writes slow down only once the item passes 400 KB
quiz.why: One item lives in one partition, and each partition tops out at 1,000 write units and 3,000 read units a second, so table-level capacity can't help. DynamoDB can move a hot item into a partition of its own, but it can't split one item. Spread the writes over several keys (a suffix per shard) and add them up on read. 400 KB is the item size limit (lesson 3).

quiz.q: A transfer debits A-1001 and credits A-2002 in DynamoDB. Which design keeps the two writes all or nothing?
options: Two UpdateItem calls with the same idempotency key
One BatchWriteItem with both updates
One TransactWriteItems with the debit's condition `balanceMinor >= :amt` and the credit
A GetItem of the balance, a check in Kotlin, then two PutItems
quiz.why: TransactWriteItems applies every action or none, and the condition is checked inside it. A batch can partly succeed and can't update with a condition; an idempotency key stops repeats, not half-done sequences; and a read outside the write races (lesson 4).

quiz.q: Why is Cassandra called a wide-column store?
options: It stores each column's values together on disk, like an analytics column store
It has no columns, only opaque values
It allows any number of columns in an index
A partition is like a wide row: a partition key and a sorted list of rows, each with its own columns
quiz.why: The name comes from Bigtable's sparse rows. It's not columnar storage, which keeps each column together for scans; Stonebraker and Pavlo describe it as a document model with one level of nesting (lessons 1 and 5).

quiz.q: A Cassandra table is keyed `((merchant_id, day), created_at)`. The busiest merchant takes 432,000 payments a day. What's the fix the guidance points to?
options: An hour bucket in the partition key, so a partition holds about 18,000 rows
A secondary index on `created_at`
Nothing: Cassandra splits large partitions across nodes
Deleting old rows every night
quiz.why: A partition never splits, and the guidance is under 100,000 rows and 100 MB. Rows = write rate × bucket length, so a smaller bucket for that table brings it under. Deletes would add tombstones, not remove rows (lesson 5).

quiz.q: Payment refunds must never exceed the payment's amount. In which designs can one write, with no transaction, check the rule and add a refund?
options: Only in a relational table with a CHECK constraint across rows
A MongoDB document with embedded refunds, or a PostgreSQL row whose jsonb holds them, each updated by one guarded statement
Only with a Cassandra logged batch
None: the rule always spans several records
quiz.why: Put the refunds inside the record and the rule is about one record, which both stores update atomically with the check in the filter or WHERE. A CHECK constraint can't see other rows, and a logged batch is atomic but not isolated (lesson 6).

quiz.q: A recursive CTE over account transfers uses `UNION ALL` and carries a `hops` column. The data has a cycle. What happens in PostgreSQL 18?
options: PostgreSQL detects the cycle and stops
It stops after 100 rounds
It runs until something cancels it; add a CYCLE clause or a path check
It raises an error before running
quiz.why: The loop stops only when a round produces no rows, and a cycle always produces more. PostgreSQL has no depth limit and detects no cycles; `CYCLE ... SET is_cycle USING path` or a path check stops it, and SQL/PGQ's `ANY SHORTEST` does the bookkeeping for you where it's available (lesson 7).

quiz.q: Which statement about graph query languages in November 2026 is accurate?
options: GraphQL is the ISO standard graph database language
PostgreSQL 19 ships SQL/PGQ's GRAPH_TABLE
Cypher was withdrawn when GQL was published
GQL (ISO/IEC 39075:2024) standardized Cypher-style patterns, and SQL/PGQ puts the same patterns inside SQL in Oracle, Spanner Graph and DuckDB
quiz.why: GQL and SQL/PGQ share one pattern language. Neo4j's Cypher 25 covers most of GQL's mandatory features. PostgreSQL reverted SQL/PGQ from 19's betas, and GraphQL is an API query language, not a database language (lessons 7, 8 and 9).

quiz.q: A GraphQL query asks for 30 payments, each with its account and the account's customer. Resolvers fetch one record per call. After you add a batching loader per type, how many backend calls does the query make?
quiz.why: One call per level: the payments, then all their distinct account ids in one call, then all the distinct customer ids in one call. Without batching it's 1 + 30 + 30 = 61, and the number grows with the page size (lesson 9).
